Pupienus (April-July AD 238). AR denarius (21mm, 3.45 gm, 7h). NGC AU 4/5 - 3/5, Fine Style. IMP C M CLOD PVPIENVS AVG, laureate, draped, and cuirassed bust of Pupienus right, seen from behind / CONCORDIA AVGG, Concordia seated left, patera in outstretched right hand, double cornucopia cradled in left arm. RIC IV.II 1. Flashy, finely detailed dies. Marcus Clodius Pupienus Maximus was elected as co-emperor to Balbinus by the senate following the death of both Gordian I and II in the tumultuous Year of the Six Emperors. While Pupienus was tasked with leading military efforts against the usurper Maximinus Thrax, tensions quickly arose between him and Balbinus. Nevertheless, Pupienus's reign would not last, as only after 99 days in office, he and his co-emperor would be hacked to death in a bath house by the Praetorian Guards. sales.title:
Balbinus (April-July AD 238). AR denarius (21mm, 2.63 gm, 1h). NGC Choice XF 5/5 - 4/5, Fine Style. Rome. IMP C D CAEL BALBINVS AVG, laureate, draped, and cuirassed bust of Balbinus right, seen from front / VICT-ORIA AVGG, Victory standing facing, head left, wreath upward in right hand, palm in left. RIC IV.II 8. Nicely detailed portrait with champagne toning. Balbinus, a figure cloaked in the shadowy annals of Roman history, briefly ascended to power in the tumultuous year 238 AD during a period known as the Year of the Six Emperors. A respected senator and seasoned politician, his reign lasted a mere 99 days, but it was marked by intrigue and political maneuvering. Appointed co-emperor alongside Pupienus, Balbinus faced the daunting task of quelling both internal strife and external threats. By minting coins with Genius Senatus, Balbinus sought to legitimize his rule as aligned with, and sanctioned by, the Senate. Associating himself with the Senate signaled that he represented the established and recognized authority in the empire. Ultimately, Balbinus was unsuccessful in winning over the populace; his administration failed to enact meaningful reforms or stabilize the economy, leaving the Roman people disillusioned with his leadership. Eventually, the populace's unrest led to a mob storming the palace. In the ensuing violence, both Balbinus and Pupienus were brutally murdered, bringing a swift and brutal conclusion to their brief co-emperorship.
